\chapter{Reading — Characters, Words, and a First Passage}
\label{ch:zh-diyi-ke}
\hlchaptermodality{29}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a Chinese character cold, find where a word ends when nothing marks it, and hold a whole passage without translating it character by character.}

Thirty-four characters in a row with no new character in them, including the first line in the book whose meaning depends on the lines before it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rén, shū, kàn, yǒu, hé, shí]{(reading) — six characters, nothing said first}

\label{lesson:ZH-C29-characters}



\begin{quote}
You have written every one of these. Not one is new.

What is new is that nobody is going to say them first.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\zh{人} \zh{书} \zh{看} \zh{有} \zh{和} \zh{十}
\end{quote}

Read down the list once. Do not count strokes — look at the whole character and let it arrive.

Again, and notice which came at once and which you had to take apart. Both are fine. The difference is what practice removes.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{What to know first}
In an alphabet a single letter is almost never a word. Here every one of these six is.

That changes what reading is. There is no sounding out: a character either lands whole or it does not land, and the only thing that moves it from the second to the first is having met it before.

Six is enough for one sitting, because six is already six words.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six characters down the list, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of the six were new? (\textbf{None.})

How many of them are whole words? (\textbf{All six.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zhōngguórén, wǒ de shū, kàn shū de …]{(reading) — six words, not six characters}

\label{lesson:ZH-C29-words}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson gave you six characters that were each a word. These are six words that are not each a character.

Every character in them is still one you have written.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\zh{中国人} \zh{我的书} \zh{看书的人} \zh{一个} \zh{十八岁} \zh{喜欢}
\end{quote}

Read down once, without stopping.

Again — and this time notice there is nothing between the characters. No space tells you where one word ends.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\zh{看书的人}} is four characters and one idea: the person who reads. You know all four, and knowing them is not the same as seeing where the join falls.

That is the work this lesson does. Mandarin writes no spaces, so a reader has to decide where a word ends, and the only tool for it is having met the word before.

\textbf{\zh{喜欢}} is the clearest case: two characters that mean nothing apart, and \emph{to like} together.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six words down the list, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many characters are in \zh{看书的人}? (\textbf{Four.}) How many words? (\textbf{One.})

What tells you where a word ends? (\textbf{Nothing on the page} — only having met it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wǒ shì zhōngguórén. wǒ yǒu yī gè míngzi.]{(reading) — the first passage}

\label{lesson:ZH-C29-diyi-ke}



\begin{quote}
Six characters, then six words. Now ten lines.

Thirty-four characters, and not one of them is new.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\zh{我是中国人} \zh{我有一个名字} \zh{我看书} \zh{我喜欢看书} \zh{我十八岁} \zh{你呢} \zh{对不对} \zh{你好} \zh{谢谢} \zh{再见}
\end{quote}

Read it through once without stopping. Do not translate as you go.

Again — and this time notice that the passage turns at line six. The first five are about the writer. The last five are addressed to you.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\zh{你呢}} is two characters and does the work of a whole English sentence: \emph{and what about you?} It only means that because of the five lines before it, which is the first time this book has asked a line to depend on what came earlier.

\textbf{\zh{我十八岁}} has no verb in it at all. Mandarin states an age by putting the number and \zh{岁} straight after the person, and a reader who waits for a verb waits forever.

This is the first whole passage the book has asked you to hold at once, and it works because every character was paid for.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the passage aloud, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which line depends on the five before it? (\textbf{\zh{你呢}})

Which line has no verb? (\textbf{\zh{我十八岁}} — and it needs none.)
\end{tcolorbox}
